newsitem.title: USA: Republicans try to head off U.S. govt shutdowns.
newsitem.headline: Republicans try to head off U.S. govt shutdowns.

text.p: A group of Republican lawmakers on Wednesday proposed a way to keep the government up and running even if Congress and the White House cannot agree on the year's budget.

Their legislation would write into law a permanent "safety net" for federal agencies to guarantee reduced, but certain, funds if the government's fiscal year starts before appropriations are signed into law.

Polls showed the public blamed Republicans more than President Bill Clinton for two partial government shutdowns, the second of which shuttered the government for 27 days last winter. The shutdowns occurred because the White House and Congress could not agree on a budget for the fiscal 1996 year that had started on Oct. 1, 1995.

The closure affected many, but not all government agencies and was most evident when tourists found Washington's museums locked and visitors were turned away from national park gates across the country.

The lawmakers said the threat of shutdown forced them ultimately to give in to the president's spending requests. Government agencies cannot operate after the October start of each fiscal year unless appropriations have been passed by Congress and signed into law by the president.

"Republicans were outfoxed by President Clinton because we were not prepared for him to use the budget process for his own political gains," Sen. John McCain, Republican of Arizona, said of budget negotiations.

After the budget agreement was reached in early 1996, House Republican leaders acknowledged that their strategy of pushing the government to a shutdown rather than accede to White House budget demands had backfired.

The legislation would guarantee government agencies the lowest of the following alternatives: the previous year's funding, the House or Senate spending bills for the year, the president's budget request or the last temporary appropriation approved by Congress.
Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens, Republican of Alaska, said he supports the bill.
